title: Fishing information website for Susaki, Japan, hit by data leak, all 3 users affected
description: Personal information for everyone posting to the site over the past year compromised. For the past week, there has been an inordinate number of hacking and data leakage from all kinds of websites, from 6.6 million people’s names, emails, and, in some cases, driver’s license info taken from major car rental and parking service Times […]
content:
Personal information for everyone posting to the site over the past year compromised.

For the past week, there has been an inordinate number of hacking and data leakage from all kinds of websites, from 6.6 million people’s names, emails, and, in some cases, driver’s license info taken from major car rental and parking service Times to the details of registered users on the Burger King app. With new leaks being reported literally every day, it’s getting to the point where you’d be in the minority to not have been affected somehow.

The latest data breach reported has come out of the city of Susaki in Kochi Prefecture. This coastal city with a population of about 20,000 people recently had their municipal fishing information website Tsuri-Baka City Susaki (Fishing-Crazy City Susaki) hacked. It appears that a company in Tokyo that manages the website’s servers was attacked and notified the fishing site on 16 October, causing them to shut down the site while an investigation is carried out.

▼ The entire Fishing-Crazy City Susaki website is down as of this writing.

As a result, everyone who used the site’s inquiry form from July 2025 to July 2026 may have had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, and details of their fishing inquiry compromised. According to the fishing bureau’s records, as many as three people may have been affected during this period. The details of the inquiries have not surfaced on the dark web but could range anywhere from how they’re bitin’ on a specific day to recommendations for a good restaurant that’ll clean and cook the day’s catch.

The current downtime is also a concern, with as many as one person potentially unable to request fishing information for the area from an official government source as opposed to other reviews on the Internet or just talking to people around town. Online comments expressed a difficulty in facing the full severity of this hack, with some resorting to humor as a defense mechanism.

“Wouldn’t it be easier just to apologize to those three people directly? Why tell all us?”
“Maybe all the victims can go on a fishing trip together.”
“This data breach is on a completely different level from anything we’ve seen before.”
“Honestly, it takes guts to come forward and admit this. I respect that.”
“I guess that’s a good thing, for some people at least.”
“It’s kind of scary that even places like that are getting hit.”
“I would like to apply for the job of the person handling their inquiries.”

I think the positive spin that can be put on all this is that it’s quite likely only a few people used the inquiry form of Fishing-Crazy City Susaki because it is such a comprehensive website and rich in detail that almost no one reading it would be left with any questions to ask. And by providing such stellar information, they managed to keep the fallout from this server attack to an absolute minimum.

It just goes to show that in these times of increasingly tenuous cyber-security, our first line of defense is quality fishing information.

Source: Kochi Shimbun Plus, Hachima Kiko

title: Beloved, 100-year-old Tokyo public bathhouse Sengenyu is about to get a second life this December
description: Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy. Public bathhouses, known as sento in Japanese, have long served as important community gathering hubs where different generations can interact with one another. Unfortunately, not all public baths are able to stay afloat […]
content:
Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy.

Public bathhouses, known as sento in Japanese, have long served as important community gathering hubs where different generations can interact with one another. Unfortunately, not all public baths are able to stay afloat in this age of rising costs and other factors. Case in point: from 2015 to 2025, the number of public bathhouses operating in Tokyo dropped from 628 to 417 locations.

Thankfully, one public bath in Tokyo’s Nerima Ward called Sengenyu is not going to join those statistics anytime soon. First opened in 1927, the third-generation previous owner was on the verge of closing the beloved community staple due to their family’s increasing age and the deteriorating facilities. However, thanks to the Tokyo Public Bathhouse Succession Matching Program offered jointly by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and the Tokyo Public Bathhouses Association, a new owner in company Ofuro Works was found. Now, instead of being demolished, Sengenyu is currently being renovated and will reopen to the public in early December.

▼ The current exterior of Sengenyu

The project includes large-scale remodeling of Sengenyu’s entrance, lobby, changing rooms, and saunas to update certain facilities.

▼ Rendition of the completed exterior, designed to blend in with the surrounding area

The lobby is particular is intended to become a spacious, relaxing entryway where patrons can soak in the warmth of the natural wood theme inside.

In addition, a new electric heater from Japanese bath company Metos will be installed within the saunas. Patrons can continue to throw water on the rocks themselves in order to increase the steam to their desired level.

These new updates don’t mean that Sengenyu will lose all of its original charm, though, as features such as the retro-style bathroom with its colorful tile art and the Shigaraki ware tanuki statue outside will be preserved in its redesign.

In a delightful community collaboration, Ofuro Works is also partnering with students at the local Nihon University College of Art to design an updated logo and mascot character based on the tanuki statue. It’s a true full-circle moment, as students from this school as well as other local universities have long been going to Sengenyu and can now leave their own personal mark on the space for many more years to come.

Finally, widespread public fundraising efforts are set to begin on November 1 through Japan’s largest crowdfunding site, Campfire. The project aims to raise 1 million yen (US$6,375) to help offset the costs of remodeling and updating the bath facilities. Financial backers will receive a towel, t-shirt, and a sneak-peek of Sengenyu behind the scenes before it reopens for business.

▼ The art students’ new logo combines the steam of a bathhouse with the puff of smoke that occurs when a tanuki transforms in Japanese folklore.

Despite the decrease in the total number of Tokyo public bathhouses, we can only hope that the statistics showing that the number of users is actually going up will allow Sengenyu and other bath facilities in the Greater Tokyo Area to flourish for 100 more years and beyond.

title: Visiting the “world’s most precarious temple” in China, where getting there is half the battle
description: Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded. Our writer Seiji recently visited China, where he got a haircut on the side of the road and did some sightseeing. One of these sights was none other than Xuankong Si, or “The Hanging Temple” in English. Its name says it all […]
content:
Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded.

Our writer Seiji recently visited China, where he got a haircut on the side of the road and did some sightseeing. One of these sights was none other than Xuankong Si, or “The Hanging Temple” in English. Its name says it all really, in that it’s a temple clinging for dear life to the side of a sheer cliff.

This temple is located in the Jinxia Gorge at the foot of Mt. Heng, known as one of China’s five great mountains. Of course, getting to a mystical temple like this was never meant to be easy and required Seiji to take a high-speed train from Beijing to Datong South Station, then drive from there into the mountains for about an hour.

▼ Seiji with his new haircut modeled after World Cup sensation Erling Haaland

It was quite a haul, but Seiji was completely enamored with the Chinese countryside. The winding mountain roads reminded him perfectly of the area where Goku first met Bulma in Dragon Ball. There was a pulse of exotic adventure everywhere he looked.

Little did he know, however, that his true battle still lay ahead. The visitor center leading into the temple area was far less mystical than other parts of his journey.

The ticket counter opens at 7:30 a.m., and Seiji arrived at 8:40. However, he was told that the tickets had already sold out. As luck would have it, tickets are sold in two batches, with 600 in the morning and another 600 in the afternoon. This meant he’d have to wait until noon to try again.

By 10 a.m.,  a significant lineup was already forming, and Seiji watched with amazement as it just got bigger…

…and bigger…

…and bigger…

…and bigger with time. By noon, it looked exactly like the line to get into Comiket.

It’s actually possible to book tickets in advance, but only for Chinese residents. This meant Seiji had no choice but to wait in line, but as he listened to two old ladies shouting at each other, he wondered why all these other people didn’t just make reservations.

Luckily, this time he could get tickets. Two types are sold: a general admission to the area for 15 yuan (US$2.25) and access to the temple itself for 100 yuan ($15). Considering how much effort it took to get this far, there was no way he was going to skip entering The Hanging Temple.

From this point, a bus ride was required, but it only took eight minutes and cost 20 yuan. But after all that traveling and waiting, he was happy to see that it was all worth it for this spectacular scenery.

This temple was mentioned on Time Magazine’s Top 10 Precarious Buildings, and since it was the only temple on the list, Seiji figures it’s safe to call it the world’s most precarious temple.

In this case, the word “precarious” doesn’t suggest poor construction or actual hazards, but a certain tilt that gives the feeling of precariousness.

This place certainly had that feeling in spades. As he walked along narrow paths jutting out from sheer cliffs that seemed to tower over him, the ground spread out far, far below him.

Seiji was never especially afraid of heights, but here he occasionally felt a little woozy and had to brace himself against the wall.

This structure was around 1,500 years old, and as is often the case with older buildings, everything feels a little smaller than usual. The railings everywhere were only about waist-height, adding to a sense that he was walking through the air.

▼ No problem there.

It truly felt like a temple in the sky, giving our writer a sensation he often felt during dreams where he was flying but then suddenly forgot how to fly and plummeted back to Earth. 

It was a one-of-a-kind experience and well-steeped in Chinese culture.

Seiji felt a sense of awe beyond most other places he’s been in his life, and would highly recommend a visit to anyone.

His only advice is to purchase the ticket to enter the temple, because it’d be a waste to travel all that way and not climb up to it. Also, make sure you arrive early because the lineup for tickets is no joke, and it’d be an even bigger waste to travel all that way and not even be able to get near Xuankong Si.

title: Baum vending machine in a Yokohama station lets us eat cake served on a luxury cruise ship
description: Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com. It takes a lot to surprise us when it comes to Japanese vending machines, considering we’ve seen everything from Sriracha to sushi meals being sold in them. While the latter might sound a bit dubious, we’ve had relatively good results […]
content:
Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com.

It takes a lot to surprise us when it comes to Japanese vending machines, considering we’ve seen everything from Sriracha to sushi meals being sold in them. While the latter might sound a bit dubious, we’ve had relatively good results with the weird and wacky, and we’re always keeping our eyes peeled for new discoveries.

The latest unusual vending machine we spotted was right outside of the ticket gates at Bashamichi Station on Yokohama’s Minatomirai Line. It was actually attracting a lot of curious glances from passersby, most likely because it was filled with Baumkuchen, the German spit cake that’s incredibly popular in Japan and usually goes by just “baum.”

▼ Cake from a vending machine somehow feels a lot safer than sushi.

A closer look at the sign revealed that this particular baum was produced by Cocotomo Farm, which makes a 100-percent gluten-free cake using homemade rice flour from Aichi Prefecture. According to the sign, its brown rice-based hard baum is even given as a welcome gift on the luxury Asuka III cruise ship–Japan’s largest passenger ship–and was being sold in this machine at a discounted price to reduce food waste.

Apparently there’s an Asuka III Meets 47 Prefectures Project, and this brand was selected as a representative for the Aichi Prefecture Room. As for why it’s being sold at this particular nondescript station in Yokohama, well, that part’s still a mystery–but perhaps it’s because there are several international cruise ship terminals in the area.

There were plenty of baum options in the vending machine, but none of the selections were for the brown rice-based hard baum variety alone. Therefore, we opted for a combo pack with a slice of that one along with a slice of the white rice-based soft baum for 650 yen (US$4.14), as well as a pack of hard baum edges for 500 yen.

▼ The machine takes cash or a variety of payment apps.

All of the baum in this machine are frozen to preserve their freshness, so our prizes were quite chilly when they first came out. Luckily, the weather was relatively warm on this particular day, and the slices of cake had thawed out well by the time we got home. Here they were in their simple, unpretentious packaging.

We were journalistically obligated to then immediately sample the slices of the soft and hard varieties, which were individually packaged.

▼ Soft baum (top) and hard baum (bottom)

The soft baum was true to its name and had a refined, moist texture. We would have never known that it was gluten-free if the packaging didn’t alert us. Meanwhile, the hard baum had the exact opposite kind of feel. It was densely packed and required some force to bite down on, being chewy at the same time. It also carried the distinctive almost nut-like flavor of brown rice. We had always assumed that all baum tasted more or less the same, but this sampling threw that notion far out the window.

Next, we broke out the hard baum edges. There were six individual pieces of slightly varying sizes packed into one bag.

The hard baum edges were, if anything, even more densely packed with flavor and texture than the soft baum and regular hard baum alike. Sure, they were rough-looking on the outside, but they hid an intense surprise on the inside.

In fact, they ended up being our favorite of the whole bunch. The value of six pieces for that price was also hard to beat.

We have no idea how long the Cocotomo Farm vending machine is going to be stationed at Bashamichi Station–but we suppose that whenever it goes away, we’ll just have to get our baum fix from the ample varieties sold at at Muji instead.

title: This curry restaurant might have the worst location in Tokyo…or maybe the best
description: Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive. There are a lot of curry restaurants to choose from in Tokyo, but Spice Curry Alk Road stands out from many of its rice-and-roux rivals by virtue of its outstanding customer reviews. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of […]
content:
Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive.

There are a lot of curry restaurants to choose from in Tokyo, but Spice Curry Alk Road stands out from many of its rice-and-roux rivals by virtue of its outstanding customer reviews. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of the top 100 curry restaurants in Tokyo based on average review scores on Tabelog, Japan’s most popular user-submitted restaurant site.

Alk Road is just a one-minute walk from Iidabashi Station, so you could say that it has a great location…but as we found out on our visit, you could also make an argument that it has the worst location for a curry restaurant in Tokyo. If you head to the restaurant’s address, you’ll find yourself in front of this building.

And yes, you will see the word “curry,” written in Japanese as カレー, on the signage.

But the writing in front of “curry,” 上等? They’re the characters for “Joto,” as in “Joto Curry,” a curry restaurant chain that is not the independent Alk Road.

So if you were to amble up here, you might think that Alk Road has gone out of business and been replaced by a Joto branch. A restaurant closing down and then a different one with the same specialty moving into the same spot isn’t all that unusual in Japan, since it lowers the renovation costs that you might have with, say, converting a yakiniku restaurant into a conveyor belt sushi joint.

However, if you look down at the entrance to Joto Curry, you’ll see that Alk Road’s name is written next to the door…

…and both Joto Curry’s and Alk Road’s names are written on the noren (cloth banner) hung above the entrance.

Things get even more confusing when you step inside, since the first floor is clearly a Joto Curry branch. If you want to find Alk Road, what you have to do is turn to your right…

…and follow the arrows pointing you up the stairs to the second floor…

…and then, finally, you’ll have arrived at Alk Road!

View this post on Instagram

Yes, Alk Road has the confusing misfortune of being a curry restaurant that you can only access by first passing part-way through a different curry restaurant, and one that’s part of a famous chain to boot.

This might seem like a recipe for constant animosity between the upstairs/downstairs neighbors, but it turns out that Joto Curry and Alk Road aren’t exactly direct competitors. Whereas Joto’s specialty is Japanese-style curry, Alk Road’s focus is on Indian-style curry, which the second-floor restaurant’s chef makes from scratch every day.

While they’re both variations on the same basic concept (curry and rice), they use different kinds of roux, and different kinds of rice too – long-grain Indian rice for Alkroad’s curry, and short-grain Japanese rice for Joto Curry’s. So among diners in Japan, these two restaurants’ offerings are scratching different culinary itches, and even if you are in a perfectly 50-50 mood as to which type of curry they were craving, Alk Road actually offers a way to enjoy both in the same meal.

One of Alk Road’s menu items is the Special Combination, a plate of curry rice in which one half is Joto’s roux and a pork cutlet, and the other is your choice of one of Alk Road’s house-specialty spice curries.

▼ Our 1,400-yen (US$8.80) Special Combination of Johto katsu curry and Alk Road chicken spice curry

You also choose between Indian and Japanese rice for the Special Combination. We asked for the Indian rice, which made for a unique mixture of flavors and textures when paired with the Japanese roux. Both curries were excellent on their own, with Alk Road’s giving us a complex mixture of spices and seasonings and Joto’s being a more straightforward spiciness with a hint of sweetness in its flavor profile, and at the center of the plate where it flowed into one another we got yet another intriguingly fresh flavor.

Should you want even more variety, Alk Road’s counter has an array of spices that you can shake onto your curry at your discretion, such as Cayenne pepper, roasted cumin, garam masala, and ajwain chili powder.

This one-of-a-kind collaborative curry combination is something that’s only possible by nature of having two different curry restaurants operating so close to one another, and through it Alk Road has cleverly turned a negative aspect of its location into a positive. So while the search for Alk Road might be a little confusing, it’s well worth going to the trouble to find, just like with a certain soft serve ice cream specialist elsewhere in Tokyo.

title: One simple unexpected recipe swap will make your Japanese-style omelets extra fluffy and juicy
description: And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still. In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet, you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). […]
content:
And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still.

In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet, you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). The cooking process is also pretty straightforward, or maybe paradoxically straightforward, since dashimaki tamago is basically an omelet that you wrap (maku) back over itself multiple times, using a rectangular frying pan if you want the traditional squared-off shape.

But just because dashimaki tamago is simple doesn’t mean it’s easy to make. The process can be surprisingly delicate, and while anyone with minimal cooking skills will be able to make dashimaki tamago that’s edible, it takes a deft hand to make dashimaki tamago with a wonderfully fluffy texture throughout its layers. So when we heard rumors of an unexpected ingredient substitution that’s supposed to make dashimaki tamago extra fluffy, we were all attentive ears and growling stomachs.

First, let’s run through the basics of how to make dashimaki tamago. You’ll need:
● 3 eggs
● 1 tablespoon of dashi (we used the type called shirodashi)
● 3 tablespoons of water

Mix them all up in a bowl, and also heat up an oiled frying pan on medium heat. Pour 1/3 of the mixture into the pan, give it a little mix with cooking chopsticks, and once it’s half-cooked, roll it to the front half of the pan. Reoil the now vacant part of the pan, add half of the ingredient mixture, and repeat the cooking and rolling process, then do it all again for the remainder of the mixture.

So what’s the cooking hack substitution we’re trying today? Using sparkling/carbonated water instead of regular water.

We heard about this idea through Asahi TV’s news/talk program Tantei! Knight Scoop, and then our reporter Natsuki Gojo headed into the SoraKitchen to test it out. Aside from the water swap, there’s only one other change to make, which is that when using the sparkling water, you mix the egg and dashi together first, and then add in the sparkling water right before cooking.

OK, let’s see if this sparkling water swap really is such a bright idea!

▼ Regular water (left) and sparkling water (right)

Starting with how the mixture of the three ingredients looked prior to cooking, as you can see in the above photo there’s a noticeable amount of fizz introduced by the sparkling water…at least initially. After stirring, though, the bubbles died down, and the regular and sparkling mixtures were equally calm.

Once Natsuki poured them into the pan, though, the bubbles came back to the sparkling mix in a big way.

Once both dashimaki tamago were done cooking, we laid them out side by side on a plate, and sure enough, the sparkling version had cooked up bigger and plumper, despite both versions having the exact same volume of ingredients.

Next we sliced off a piece from each to examine their cross-sections, and were happy to see that the sparkling water substitution had produced exactly the sort of results we’d been hoping for!

The regular-water version had congealed towards the bottom of the roll, but the sparkling dashimaki tamago had maintained a nice network of little air pockets while cooking, and those had made it fluffier. It wasn’t just the texture that had been enhanced, either. The sparkling dashimaki tamago was juicier too.

Emboldened by this success, Natsuki decided to whip up one more batch of dashimaki tamago to test out another rumor she’d heard for further fluffiness. This time, instead of using three tablespoons of sparkling water, she used 175 milliliters (5.9 ounces), or roughly 10 tablespoons.

Unsurprisingly, this resulted in even more bubbles at the pre-mix and cooking stages, and Natsuki found herself worried that the mixture might be too watery to cook up properly.

But those fears turned out to be unnecessary, and this high-volume sparkling water version was the fluffiest and juiciest of all three she cooked.

▼ Sparkling water dashimaki tamago (left) and high-volume sparkling water dashimaki tamago (right)

Natsuki herself is quick to point out that she doesn’t have a ton of experience cooking her own dashimaki tamago, so we’re not saying that using sparkling water is a must for good results. At the same time, her relative inexperience proves that you don’t have to be an expert to benefit from this simple ingredient swap, so if you’re looking to make your Japanese-style omelets as fluffy as you can, this is definitely worth giving a shot.

title: Japan getting a brand-new batch of Pokémon manhole covers in eastern prefecture this fall
description: Five new reasons for Pokémon fans to head north from Tokyo. Fall is a fantastic time to take a trip to Gunma Prefecture. Located about two hours north of Tokyo, Gunma gets some beautiful autumn foliage and it also boasts some of east Japan’s finest hot springs, making for a great combo of crisp afternoon […]
content:
Five new reasons for Pokémon fans to head north from Tokyo.

Fall is a fantastic time to take a trip to Gunma Prefecture. Located about two hours north of Tokyo, Gunma gets some beautiful autumn foliage and it also boasts some of east Japan’s finest hot springs, making for a great combo of crisp afternoon walks followed by a rejuvenatingly warm soak.

As of this fall, there’s one more reason to head to Gunma. Well, five actually, as the prefecture is getting five new Pokémon manhole covers!

The Pokéfuta/Poké Lids project is a series of artistic one-of-a-kind manhole covers highlighting local communities, helping to draw visitors to lesser-known but still charming parts of Japan. The covers all feature Pocket Monster species and local scenery or representative products such as produce or handicrafts. For example, the Gunma town of Shimonita takes great pride in the quality of the green onions that its farmers grow, so naturally its Pokéfuta, installed in front of the Coconita building next to Shimonita Station, features Farfetch’d, Galarian Farfetch’d, and Sirfetch’d.

Boltund naturally feels at home playing in front of Yamba Dam, a towering hydroelectric facility in the town of Naganohara. Joining the Electric-type on this cover, which will be at the Yamba Furusato-kan michi no eki (“road station” local products shop) are Meltan and Seaking, creating further tie-ins with the water/engineering theme.

Zigzagoon, in both standard and Galarian forms, appears on the Pokéfuta for the Tsutsujigaoka Fureai Center, located inside Tsutsujigaoka Park in the town of Tatebayashi. This one might actually be best to wait until spring to visit, as tsutsuji is the Japanese word for azalea, and the park contains some 10,000 bushes on which the seasonal flowers bloom.

Dunsparce and Shiftry can be seen hanging out on their manhole cover at the entrance to the hiking trail that leads to Fukiware Falls in the town of Numata, placed next to the parking area that hikers can use. Shiftry is here because his design is based on the tengu (crow spirits) of Japanese folklore, who are often depicted using giant leaves or fans to create strong gusts of wind. Tengu are prominently featured in the folklore surrounding Numata’s Miroku Temple on Mt. Kasho, which claims to have the largest tengu mask in all of Japan.

And finally, as you board or exit the Shibukawa Ikaho Ropeway at Hototogisu Station in the town of Shibukawa, you’ll be able to say hi to Zapdos, who, being a Flying-type Pokémon, can enjoy expansive views and mountain scenery without having to ride one of the ropeway’s gondolas.

Festive cheer is here, with mugs, tumblers, candles and keychains you won’t find at any other time of year.

That means it’s time for Starbucks to start bringing us some holiday cheer, and this year it’s doing that with a massive collection of festive goods based around the theme of “Colours of Holiday“.

Red, green, white and gold are the main colours in the collection, with Bearistas and ribbons adding an extra touch of cuteness and glamour to the festivities. There are a lot of wonderful surprises in store, including a trio of exclusive candles, so let’s take a closer look at everything in the range, which Starbucks says will “brighten your heart for the holiday season”.

title: Cup Noodle launching “isekai” crossover line featuring flavors from outside instant ramen world
description: An isekai trip for your taste buds, no truck accident required. Isekai translates to “alternate world,” but within the Japanese pop culture sphere it’s also the name of a genre of anime, novels, and other media in which someone gets transported from our mundane plane of existence to a realm with new adventures waiting for […]
content:
An isekai trip for your taste buds, no truck accident required.

Isekai translates to “alternate world,” but within the Japanese pop culture sphere it’s also the name of a genre of anime, novels, and other media in which someone gets transported from our mundane plane of existence to a realm with new adventures waiting for them. A salaryman might be whisked away to a second life as a spacefaring explorer, or a schoolgirl might awaken to find herself reborn in a kingdom where she’s now part of a web of romantic courtly intrigue.

But now it’s Cup Noodles’ turn to get isekai-ed, as Nissin has announced three new flavors that combine their instant noodles with other beloved food brands from outside the cup ramen world.

First up for the Cup Noodle Isekai Gattai series (gattai meaning “combination”) is a collaboration between the standard Cup Noodle flavor and Gindaco, one of Japan’s most popular takoyaki (octopus ball) chains.

The familiar Cup Noodle broth gets enhancements of extra dashi (bonito stock), and the customary takoyaki ingredients of powdered seaweed, pickled ginger, plus flavors evocative of the sweet sauce that’s squirted on the dumplings. Inside the cup, Cup Noodle’s iconic “mystery meat” is joined by the similarly mysterious-sounding “octopus-style balls.” There’s also an extra packet of oil on the side to add after the noodles cook as a salute to the oil that Gindako adds to its takoyaki.

Next up is a meeting of the worlds of Curry Cup noodle and Karamucho, Japan’s spiciest mass-market crisp potato stick snacks.

The already piquant curry broth gets its heat turned up a notch with the addition of chilies, plus garlic too. Floating in that spicy/savory mix are pieces of chili-spiced potato, mystery meat, and carrots.

And finally, Seafood Cup Noodle joins forces with Gohan Desu Yo, a brand of simmered seaweed. Gohan Desu Yo is usually eaten by adding a small spoonful to a bowl of white rice, but for this team-up you get a packet of simmered seaweed paste to squeeze into the broth after cooking. That broth is based on the Seafood Cup Noodle, but with extra seaweed, and the oceanic theme continues with pieces of squid and imitation crab, plus cabbage, egg, and green onion.

All three varieties are priced at 259 yen (US$1.65) scheduled to go on sale November 9.

title: Japanese snack lovers may soon be spore-ting the latest crowdfunded confectionery tech
description: Play that fung-ky music. From creepy penguins hatching from eggs to flying balls of chaos, Japan likes to jump on the latest quirky trends, and if history is anything to go by, people will soon be putting fungi in their ears. If you have ever browsed the snack aisle of a Japanese convenience store, there’s […]
content:
Play that fung-ky music.

From creepy penguins hatching from eggs to flying balls of chaos, Japan likes to jump on the latest quirky trends, and if history is anything to go by, people will soon be putting fungi in their ears. If you have ever browsed the snack aisle of a Japanese convenience store, there’s a chance that you might have encountered Kinoko no Yama, bite-sized treats consisting of a crunchy biscuit stem topped with a chocolate mushroom cap. Now, imagine putting one in your ear.

Rather than being the latest dietary trend, or attempting to commune deeper with nature through the chocolate mycelia, what appears to be the start of a fungal colony growing out of your head is in fact the second-generation Kinoko no Yama Wireless Earphones Pro, a tech accessory that looks like you’re using actual confectionery as audio equipment.

The concept originally started as a playful visual joke on social media, but after an overwhelming response from netizens demanding to know where they could buy a pair, Kagomedia collaborated with Kinoko no Yama’s maker Meiji to turn them into a reality. The first batch of 3,500 units launched on the Japanese crowdfunding platform Makuake in early 2024 and famously sold out in a shocking ten minutes.

▼ Achieving 9,836 percent of its one million yen goal.

Two and a half years later, these chocolate earbuds are making a comeback from November 1, with a new revival project for the updated 2027 Pro model. If the campaign sees at least 1,000 people pledge that they want a pair, the second generation will officially go into production, but this time they will be made-to-order without a strict limit on quantities, so all those who want will be able to get their hands and ears on them.

Despite looking like a novelty gimmick, these earbuds pack some serious tech, with upgraded audio tuning and gold-plated touch sensors. The most ambitious feature though is the built-in AI simultaneous translation covering 144 global languages and dialects. So while you might look like you’re trying to store your snacks in your ears for later to onlookers, you could be able to understand nearly 150 languages in real time.

The case itself is designed to mirror the original snack box, complete with a pop-up tray where the two little mushrooms rest inside.

If you, like your 3,500 predecessors, want some fungi in your head, you’ll need to check out Makuake on November 1 at 12:00 p.m., where for the first 24 hours, the first 1,000 pairs of earphones will be sold at the same price as the first-generation (29,800 yen [US$188.96]). The next 2,000 pairs can be bought for 31,800 yen, and the following 2,000 for 33,000 yen. The last possible discount is for 3,000 pairs at 34,800 yen before each unit is sold for its regular price of 36,300 yen with no quantity limits as long as the order is placed before December 13, 2026, after which you will not be able to purchase these any more.

Whether you find the design quirky or strange, it’s a high-quality blend of everyday Japanese pop culture with high-tech innovation, so there’s no need to panic the next time you spot someone on the train with mushrooms sprouting from their ears.

title: Japan’s super cute tanuki bread skips tricks, promises to be treat for your eyes and taste buds
description: You can trust this tanuki to be as sweet on the inside as it looks on the outside. In Japanese folklore, tanuki are tricksters. There’s nothing they love more than playing pranks on us unsuspecting humans, and that image of them even extends to Japanese cuisine. “Tanuki soba” and “tanuki udon” are styles of noodles […]
content:
You can trust this tanuki to be as sweet on the inside as it looks on the outside.

In Japanese folklore, tanuki are tricksters. There’s nothing they love more than playing pranks on us unsuspecting humans, and that image of them even extends to Japanese cuisine. “Tanuki soba” and “tanuki udon” are styles of noodles topped with tempura flakes only, because those crafty racoon dogs have tricked you by already eating the shrimp or veggies that would ordinarily be inside the tempura.

But at the same time, tanuki are really, really cute, and thankfully it’s this aspect that Japanese bakery Kimuraya has chosen to focus on for the treats that’ll be coming out of their ovens next month.

Called Tanuki-kun (-kun being a form of address in Japanese that’s friendlier and more familiar than -san), these baked goods are the polar opposite from tanuki soba/udon in terms of filling generosity. Inside the bun is a mixture of caramel cream and chocolate chips, promising a richly sweet and satisfying flavor profile with an interesting texture too.

On the outside, the tanuki’s facial features are made of chocolate, and the mask-like marking around its eyes, and part of its ears too, are rendered with a chocolate biscuit dough.

Kimuraya is a little on the premium-priced side for a Japanese bakery, and the 400-yen (US$2.50) Tanuki-kun is likewise a little more expensive than the average bakery treat, but with something that looks this delicious and adorable, we can make room in our snack budget. The Tanuki-kun goes on sale at Kimuraya bakeries from November 1, but can also be ordered through the Kimuraya online store as of October 28.

title: Shinkansen online ticketing service reports customer data leak
description: Online reservation system handles tickets for Shinkansen’s “Golden Route” and Kyushu. If you’re planning to take a ride on the Shinkansen, the Smart EX online ticketing service is a handy utility. Managed by Shinkansen operator Central Japan Railway Company/JR Central, Smart EX lets you book seats on bullet trains running in eastern and western Japan, […]
content:
Online reservation system handles tickets for Shinkansen’s “Golden Route” and Kyushu.

If you’re planning to take a ride on the Shinkansen, the Smart EX online ticketing service is a handy utility. Managed by Shinkansen operator Central Japan Railway Company/JR Central, Smart EX lets you book seats on bullet trains running in eastern and western Japan, as well as the southwestern island of Kyushu. A wide selection of credit cards can be used for payment, and the Smart EX mobile app can provide you with a QR code so that you don’t have to fuss around with a paper ticket.

Unfortunately, it’s not just travelers that have found Smart EX alluring, but hackers too, as JR Central has announced a data breach has resulted in personal information of roughly 170,000 Smart EX users being leaked.

The incident stems from another security breach earlier this month at Yumirulink, a digital marketing and email forwarding service involved in the routing of some Smart EX messages.

Thankfully, the Smart EX user data that was stolen is of a limited scope. According to JR Central’s statement, hackers were able to obtain the users’ names, email addresses, member IDs/screen names, and membership types. Date of birth, home addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers and expiration dates were not leaked, the company says. In addition, JR Central says that only the renderings of users’ names in Japanese katakana phonetic characters were leaked, and other forms were not compromised. However, it’s somewhat unclear if this assertion applies only to non-katakana Japanese text (i.e. kanji-character) versions of user names, or if it also is meant to cover names written in the Latin alphabet, since as of this writing the Smart EX website only has a statement regarding the data leak on its Japanese-language page, with no mention of it on the service’s English site.

JR Central’s statement also says that the data breach was not connected to auto-generated emails such as those that Smart EX sends to confirm bookings or customer-initiated schedule changes, and instead is related to emails sent for things such as sale promotions or altered timetable notifications following the recent Kumamoto earthquake.

Collectively, the Smart EX system covers Shinkansen bookings for bullet trains operated by JR Central, JR West, and JR Kyushu, which together stretch from Tokyo through Osaka, Kyoto, and Hiroshima on to Fukuoka and then down to Kagoshima. So if you’ve used the service to book a Shinkansen ticket along that network, it’s probably a good idea to keep an eye on your various other online accounts in the coming days, just in case someone out there has some of your personal data.

title: Starbucks Japan releases “Let’s Par-TEA!” Frappuccino and drinks for the holiday season
description: Each beverage has its own unique character so you can choose which one you’d like to party with. With the holiday season fast approaching, Starbucks is bringing the party spirit to its stores in Japan with a trio of new drinks based around the theme of “Let’s par-TEA!” As the name suggests, the three new holiday […]
content:
Each beverage has its own unique character so you can choose which one you’d like to party with.

With the holiday season fast approaching, Starbucks is bringing the party spirit to its stores in Japan with a trio of new drinks based around the theme of “Let’s par-TEA!” As the name suggests, the three new holiday drinks shine a spotlight on tea, with strawberry, royal milk tea and Earl Grey chocolate featuring in the beverages.

The three stars of this tea party each have their own distinct character, so you can choose the one that best suits your mood. Those wanting an elegant pick-me-up can opt for the Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte, which combines robust black tea with the smooth sweetness of oolong tea and the floral fragrance of jasmine tea, finished with a subtle hint of apricot.

▼ Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte (Tall size only, 638 yen [US$4.03] for takeout; 650 yen for dine-in)

The blended tea base is joined by sweetened fresh cream and a topping of strawberry-flavoured mousse and freeze-dried strawberries. The rich aroma of the chain’s famous Joyful Medley blend, which is reminiscent of apricot jam, is layered with creamy sweetness, while the finish remains refreshing, allowing you to enjoy a variety of tastes and aromas throughout the beverage.

▼ Earl Grey Chocolate Frappuccino (Tall size only, 678 yen takeout; 690 yen dine-in)

Those wanting a little more playfulness can reward themselves with this tea-and-chocolate Frappuccino, which combines aromatic Earl Grey with rich chocolate sauce and crunchy chocolate chips. It has a mellow, layered flavour, with the gentle fragrance of bergamot and the taste of black tea spreading through the palate with every sip, while the chocolate chips add crunchy textural contrast, capturing the playful spirit of the holiday season.

▼ Royal Milk Tea (609 yen takeout; 620 yen dine-in)

Finally, we have a rich, blended milk tea that combines milk with an original blend of three teas: Darjeeling, Assam and Ceylon. The full-bodied flavour of the tea harmonises with the mellow creaminess of the milk, creating a rich and rewarding taste that tea lovers will fall in love with.

As an extra special holiday treat, Starbucks is also adding a cookie option, so you can add more flavour and a dash of cuteness to any iced beverage that’s topped with whipped cream or mousse foam.

▼ Be a Santa Cookie Topping (69 yen takeout; 70 yen dine-in)

The “Be a Santa Cookie Topping” has a buttery aroma and crisp yet crumbly shortbread texture. The three designs – a present, a Christmas tree and a Santa hat – are provided at random so, like a Christmas present, you won’t know what you’re getting until it’s given to you by the barista.

While the cookie topping will be available while stocks last from 2-19 November, the drinks will be on the menu for a limited (but unspecified) time from 2 November.

title: Japanese government still lists refusing to pay for dates as a form of domestic violence
description: Once again, there’s a lot of nuance that’s lost in the attempt to be succinct. As you can probably guess from its name, the Japanese government’s Gender Equality Bureau isn’t a fan of imbalance in interpersonal relationships. What is surprising to many people, though, is the bureau’s assertion that “not paying for any dating expenses” […]
content:
Once again, there’s a lot of nuance that’s lost in the attempt to be succinct.

As you can probably guess from its name, the Japanese government’s Gender Equality Bureau isn’t a fan of imbalance in interpersonal relationships. What is surprising to many people, though, is the bureau’s assertion that “not paying for any dating expenses” is committing an act of domestic violence.

On its website, the bureau lists four categories of “dating domestic violence.” Examples of “physical violence” are pretty obvious – striking, pulling hair, throwing objects, that sort of thing. “Sexual violence,” the bureau says, includes coerced sex, refusal to use contraception, and nonconsensual naked photography or video recording. “Psychological violence” is described as making insulting or disrespectful remarks, forbidding a romantic partner from seeing their friends, or monitoring their email communications.

It’s bureau discussion of “economic violence,” though, that’s been raising some eyebrows online in Japan this week. While one could argue that this is using the word “violence” in its broadest possible sense, most of the examples are things that would be considered wrong under basic common sense/decency, such as not paying back money borrowed from a romantic partner, taking money from their bank account without permission, and forbidding them to work outside the home or forcing them to quit their job. But then there’s this example of economic violence:

“Not paying for any dating expenses.”

Japan may not have a reputation for being the most chivalrous society, and going Dutch, or warikan, as it’s called in Japanese, is more common in casual dating here than it is in some other countries. That said, it’s not at all unusual for guys to pay for everything on a date with a girl, and the government of Japan saying that this is a form of domestic violence has been provoking a lot of responses online to a recent Twitter post pointing out the bureau’s stance.

“Yeah, it’s practically theft, so it’s obviously a form of domestic abuse.”
“Wait, I’ve never made a girl pay on a date, so does that mean that I’ve been subjected to economic violence in the eyes of the government?”
“There are a lot of guys who are the victim of this kind of domestic abuse.”
“Does this make guys who habitually treat the girl on dates masochists for actively encouraging dating domestic violence?”
“Let’s all make sure to properly split the bill, because the government has said that anything other than that is considered economic violence, OK?”
“That’ll show all those gold-digger girls who hang out in Tokyo’s Minato Ward.”
“This is wonderful for men. I think all us guys are thinking ‘Hey, can’t you pitch in a little?’ but we can’t say it to the girl because we’re trying to look cool.”
“Coerced treating is a crime.”
“I think they mean it’s wrong for both guys and girls to refuse to pay for dating expenses.”

There’s probably at least a little wry humor behind some of those comments, but the last two are the ones that really get to the heart of the matter. As clarified by a spokesperson for the Gender Equality Bureau when this example of economic violence also became a topic of online discussion a few years ago, the bureau recognizes that “Both men and women can be victims of this kind of violence” and that “If both sides are OK with [one person not paying], it’s not domestic violence.” It’s when one person attempts to force their partner to shoulder all of the dating costs against their will that it crosses the line into unacceptable behavior, or when someone demands to be reimbursed for past dating expenses that, at the time, they offered to pay for.

▼ Just like going to a butcher shop on a date is fine if that’s what both you and your sweetheart are into, so too is it OK if you’re in agreement that you’ll be treating her to a half-kilo of ground beef.

In other words, the bureau’s guidelines are more about discouraging someone from unilaterally declaring “We’re going out, and you’re going to pay for me” or becoming verbally abusive if asked to chip in, not shaming someone for consistently accepting offers to be treated. But while we’re on the subject of “other words,” as mentioned above, this is not the first time the vague language used on the bureau’s website regarding who pays on a date has caused confusion, and the list of examples being followed by the declaration that “All of these are violence” leaves the door open to misinterpretation that context and a couple’s specific circumstances are irrelevant. The statement has remained on the site in its current form since 2018, so maybe it’s time for an update that puts a finer point on things.

Source: Gender Equality Bureau, Hachima Kiko, Twitter/@anzuchanw

content:
Kiki’s Delivery Service scene-stealer is adorably transfixed by Donguri Kyowakoku’s latest homeware offering.

Any branch of Ghibli specialty shop chain Donguri Kyowakoku will be filled with amazing merch from the anime studio’s films, but a few locations are extra-special thanks to their inclusion of items from the Donguri Closet sub-brand. As the name alludes to, Donguri Closet’s focus is on fashion and home décor. The designs have an elegant coziness to them, making them the sort of things that, without being flashy, will catch the eyes of fans as soon as they step into the room…and, in this case, catch the eyes of Kiki’s Delivery Service’s Jiji too.

So what’s got Kiki’s black cat companion so captivated? A recreation of an oil lamp seen in the home of Osono, the kindly baker who Kiki and Jiji rent a room from after arriving in the city where the anime’s story takes place. Though made of resin and ABS for extra sturdiness, the intricate details and delicate coloring give it a look evocative of antique porcelain.

The clear top section of the lamp is made of glass, but since the logistics hassles and safety risks of burning an actual oil lamp can be a hassle to deal with, this is an electric light. The designers have cleverly hid the main power switch on the underside of the base, though, to better sell the illusion of old-timey-ness, and the light can be turned on or off with a tap of your finger thanks to a touch sensor embedded in the lamp.

Officially called the Kiki’s Delivery Service Mini Lamp-Mitsumeru Jiji (“Transfixed Jiji”), the piece is 12.8 centimeters (5 inches) tall and 11.2 centimeters wide, putting it right in that sweet spot where it’s neither too small to be noticed nor too big to be in the way. Priced at 13,200 yen (US$83), it’ll be available at select Donguri Kyowakoku stores in Tokyo (Ikebukuro, Skytree Town Solamachi), Nagoya (Takashimaya Gate Tower Mall), Osaka (Lucua Osaka), Fukuoka (Canal City Hakata), and Sapporo (Sapporo Parco), as well as through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here starting October 31.

content:
Combining palanquins and muscle suits to make historic sites accessible for all.

Along the eastern shores of Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest freshwater lake, in Shiga is the city of Hikone, home to one of only twelve castles in Japan with its original main keep still standing.

However, reaching the top is not a casual stroll, being guarded by 140 steep, irregular stone steps explicitly designed to exhaust invading samurai, and now those same steps present a modern dilemma.

Being a National Special Historic Site, and a possible candidate for UNESCO World Cultural Heritage status in 2028, how can the site be made more accessible for visitors who use wheelchairs or have mobility impairments, especially when pouring concrete ramps over 17th-century masonry isn’t exactly an option that would be enthusiastically received?

On October 19, Hikone City staff and volunteers conducted a trial, where they took turns acting as carriers, carrying wheelchair users up to the main enclosure (honmaru) using a traditional wooden mountain palanquin (yamakago). The trek covered a 285-meter (935-foot) round-trip with a 50-meter (165-foot) vertical rise and an average 18-percent incline, which is not an easy feat for two people to do.

So, to lighten the load for the team of six carriers, trial participants strapped on state-of-the-art, non-motorized wearable assist suits, with two wearing the Muscle Suit Soft-Power Easy-Lift and four equipping the Mediaid Firm Guard Waist EX Hard.

▼Muscle Suit Soft-Power Easy-Lift

▼Mediaid Firm Guard Waist EX Hard

The reaction from the carriers was enthusiastic, receiving comments like:
“Because I injured my lower back in the past, wearing it gave me a real sense of security.”
“It is attached at the base of the knees, but when standing upright it is loose, so it does not get in the way of going up and down the stairs.”
“The moment I took it off, I realized just how much it had been helping me.”

Standing up while balancing a palanquin on your shoulders normally feels like tipping backward, causing some difficulty in maintaining balance, but the back-and-leg support makes rising smooth and stable.

Beyond opening up easier physical access to a historic tourist site, the trial offered a glimpse into an exciting future for Japanese tourism, with accompanying curators explaining the history and scenery of the location, creating an opportunity for visitors to get a taste of what it would be like to travel around the mountain like nobility in the time of the samurai.

Similarly, it could also open up another bucket-list item for many travelers along with sitting on the back of a human-powered rickshaw, being chauffeured around Japan’s historical districts. If wearable assist suits can help bridge the gap between 17th-century architecture and 21st-century accessibility, it opens up countless possibilities for historic castles, mountain temples, and heritage sites all across Japan.

title: Real-world Legend of Zelda treasures, Heart Container lights and Ruppe pouches, coming soon [Pics]
description: Whether you’re restoring your energy at home or out adventuring in the world, these Hyrulian artifacts will be ready to help. content:
Whether you’re restoring your energy at home or out adventuring in the world, these Hyrulian artifacts will be ready to help.

Nintendo fans already have November 5 circled on their calendars, since that’s when the long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time goes on sale for the Switch 2. That’s not the only cool Zelda-related release coming up in November though, with Japanese fashion and interior company Takarajimasha, whose name means “treasure island company,” releasing two creations based on treasure from Nintendo’s fantasy franchise.

The first item is a replica of the coveted Heart Container, which has been extending the hero Link’s maximum life bar since the very start of the series. Takarajimasha’s version is modeled on the version seen in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom with its arabesque gold framing.

While this real-world won’t instantly increase your longevity or resilience, it can provide illumination, as it’s actually a 9-centimeter (3.5-inch) tall lamp that produces a warm red glow when switched on.

The designers know that you will want to hold this in your hands, so the lamp can be detached from the base.

▼ Though you’ll have to hum Zelda’s traditional four-note “treasure found” fanfare yourself.

Because of their value and rarity, Heart Containers are something that players search high and low for in exploring the games’ realms, but Takarajimasha also wants to salute the most common of Zelda treasures, the humble Rupee.

The green Ruppe, the smallest-denomination of Hyrulian currency, is something you’ll collect hundreds of, if not thousands, during a playthrough of one of the Zelda games, and yet, it’s still sure to bring a smile to you, or any fellow fans, when one shows up in our world as a zippered silicone pouch.

The designers bill is as a komono ire, a Japanese term whose closest English equivalent would be “accessory pouch,” but really refers to a pouch for storing any small items, such as earbuds, cosmetics, or even bite-sized snacks.

There’s a strap in case you want to use it as a bag charm, and you’ll also find The Legend of Zelda, written in Japanese, on the Rupee’s underside.

A quirk of the Japanese publishing industry is that fashion and lifestyle magazines sometimes come with some sort of fashion/lifestyle item bundled with them. Sometimes these are so popular that they overshadow the edition of the periodical, so, noticing this, companies like Takarajimasha that specialize in such bundled items sometimes flip the script and make the items the primary product and toss in a mini magazine as a supplementary freebie. Both the Heart Container Interior Light and the Rupee Silicone Pouch are being offered in this format, branded as “Books” and sold together with an eight-page booklet of undisclosed but presumably Zelda-related nature.

The Heart Container light is priced at 3,839 yen (US$24) and the Rupee pouch at 2,992 yen. They both go on sale November 2 and can be ordered, here and here, through the Takarajimasha online shop as well as through select branches of convenience store chain Lawson.
